questions.question: What does the Legendre symbol (a/p) equal when a is a non-zero quadratic residue mod prime p?
options: 0, by convention for non-zero residues that are perfect squares
+1, indicating a is a quadratic residue modulo the prime p
−1, indicating a is a quadratic non-residue modulo the prime
a itself reduced mod p, with no further normalization applied
questions.explanation: Legendre symbol: (a/p) = +1 if a is a QR mod p, −1 if non-QR, 0 if p | a.

questions.question: How is the Legendre symbol computed via Euler's criterion?
options: (a/p) ≡ a^((p+1)/2) (mod p), giving the value as a residue itself
(a/p) ≡ a^((p−1)/2) (mod p), interpreting the result as ±1
(a/p) ≡ a^(p−2) (mod p), the Fermat inverse formula for primes
(a/p) ≡ a^p mod (p−1), reducing the exponent mod the order
questions.explanation: Euler: a^((p−1)/2) ≡ (a/p) (mod p), where the result is +1 or −1.

questions.question: The Jacobi symbol (a/n) generalizes Legendre to which moduli?
options: Any odd positive composite n, defined multiplicatively over its prime factors
Any even composite n, computable via factoring the smallest prime factor
Any prime power p^k, generalizing Legendre to higher exponents only
Any positive integer n, including evens via a special factor of two rule
questions.explanation: Jacobi (a/n) for odd positive n = p₁^a₁ · … · pₖ^aₖ is defined as ∏ (a/pᵢ)^aᵢ — product of Legendre symbols.

questions.question: If Jacobi (a/n) = −1, what can you conclude about a's quadratic residuosity mod n?
options: a is definitely a quadratic non-residue mod n (no x with x² ≡ a exists)
a is definitely a quadratic residue mod n with exactly two roots
a may be either a residue or non-residue; Jacobi is inconclusive here
a divides n exactly, so the symbol takes the conventional value zero
questions.explanation: (a/n) = −1 ⇒ at least one Legendre factor is −1 ⇒ a is non-QR mod some pᵢ ⇒ a is non-QR mod n. The +1 case is ambiguous.

questions.question: Quadratic reciprocity (Gauss) states for distinct odd primes p, q:
options: (p/q) · (q/p) = (−1)^((p−1)/2 · (q−1)/2), letting you flip the symbol
(p/q) + (q/p) = 0 always, regardless of the parity of p and q involved
(p/q) = (q/p) holds unconditionally for any distinct odd prime pair
(p/q) · (q/p) = +1 unless p = q = 3 (mod 4), the exceptional case only
questions.explanation: QR: (p/q)(q/p) = (−1)^((p−1)/2·(q−1)/2). Flip is free unless both p, q ≡ 3 (mod 4), then symbols flip sign.

questions.question: Compute the Jacobi symbol (3/35) where 35 = 5·7.
options: +1, since (3/5)(3/7) = (−1)·(−1) = +1 via Euler on each prime
−1, since (3/5)·(3/7) = (−1)·(+1) makes the product negative
0, since 3 divides 35 evenly leaving no quadratic residue class
+3, which is 3 itself unreduced under multiplicative composition

questions.question: Solovay-Strassen primality test uses Jacobi how?
options: n is prime iff Jacobi(a/n) ≡ a^((n−1)/2) (mod n) for every base a coprime to n
n is prime iff Jacobi(a/n) = +1 for at least half the bases a in [1, n−1]
n is composite iff Jacobi(a/n) divides a^(n−1) mod n for some base a
n is composite iff Jacobi(n/a) = 0 for any prime a less than √n
questions.explanation: Solovay-Strassen: pick random a, compute Jacobi(a/n) and a^((n−1)/2) mod n. If they disagree, n is composite. Probabilistic, error ≤ 1/2 per round.

questions.question: An attacker uses Jacobi(a/n) = +1 on Goldwasser-Micali ciphertexts to do what?
options: Distinguish pseudosquares from real QRs — believed as hard as factoring n
Recover the plaintext bit directly from the ciphertext without factoring
Compute the modular square root of the ciphertext using Tonelli-Shanks
Factor n by exploiting collisions between Jacobi and Legendre evaluations
questions.explanation: GM encrypts bit 0 as a true QR mod n (Jacobi=+1) and bit 1 as a pseudosquare (Jacobi=+1, but non-QR). Distinguishing them is the QR Problem — as hard as factoring.
